title: III. A Little Demon
paragraphs: Going in to see Lise, he found her half-reclining in the invalid chair she'd been wheeled around in back when she couldn't walk. She didn't move to greet him, but her sharp, keen eyes fixed on his face at once. There was a feverish look in her eyes, her face pale and yellowish. Alyosha was startled by how much she'd changed in three days. She was noticeably thinner. She didn't hold out her hand to him. He touched her thin, long fingers, lying motionless on her dress, then sat down facing her without a word.
"I know you're in a hurry to get to the prison," Lise said curtly, "and mamma's kept you sitting there for hours — she's just been telling you all about me and Yulia."
"How do you know that?" Alyosha asked.
"I was listening. Why are you staring at me? I wanted to listen, and I did listen, there's no harm in that. I'm not apologizing."
"You're upset about something?"

"On the contrary, I'm very happy. I've just been thinking, for the thirtieth time, what a good thing it is that I turned you down and won't be your wife. You're not fit to be a husband. If I married you and gave you a note to take to the man I loved after you, you'd take it, and you'd be sure to deliver it, and bring back an answer too. Even at forty, you'd still be carrying my love letters for me."
She suddenly laughed.
"There's something spiteful about you, and yet something open-hearted too," Alyosha said, smiling at her.

"The open-heartedness is that I'm not ashamed of myself in front of you. What's more, I don't want to feel ashamed in front of you — just you. Alyosha, why is it I don't respect you? I'm very fond of you, but I don't respect you. If I respected you, I wouldn't talk to you without shame, would I?"
"No."
"But do you believe that I'm not ashamed with you?"
"No, I don't believe it."
Lise laughed nervously again; she spoke quickly.
"I sent your brother, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, some sweets in prison. Alyosha, you know, you're actually quite pretty! I'm going to love you terribly for letting me stop loving you so quickly."
"Why did you send for me today, Lise?"
"I wanted to tell you about a longing I have. I'd like someone to torture me — marry me, and then torture me, deceive me, and leave. I don't want to be happy."
"You're in love with disorder?"

"Yes, I want disorder. I keep wanting to set the house on fire. I keep imagining how I'd creep up and set fire to it on the sly — it would have to be on the sly. They'll try to put it out, but it'll go on burning. And I'll know, and say nothing. Ah, what nonsense! And how bored I am!"
She waved her hand with a look of disgust.
"It's your luxurious life," Alyosha said softly.
"Is it better, then, to be poor?"
"Yes, it's better."

"That's what your monk taught you. That's not true. Let me be rich, and everyone else poor — I'll eat sweets and drink cream and not give any to anyone else. Ach, don't talk, don't say anything," she shook her hand at him, though Alyosha hadn't opened his mouth. "You've told me all that before, I know it by heart. It bores me. If I'm ever poor, I'll murder somebody, and even if I'm rich, maybe I'll murder someone too — why just sit around doing nothing! But do you know, I'd love to go reap the rye, cut it myself? I'll marry you, and you'll turn into a peasant, a real peasant — we'll keep a colt, shall we? Do you know Kalganov?"
"Yes."

"He's always wandering around, dreaming. He says, 'Why live in real life? It's better to dream. You can dream up the most wonderful things, but real life is a bore.' But he'll get married for all that; he's already been flirting with me. Can you spin tops?"
"Yes."

"Well, he's just like a top: he wants to be wound up and set spinning, and then lashed, lashed, lashed with a whip. If I marry him, I'll keep him spinning his whole life. Aren't you ashamed to be seen with me?"
"No."
"You're terribly cross with me because I won't talk about holy things. I don't want to be holy. What will they do to a person in the next world for the worst sin? You must know all about that."
"God will judge you," Alyosha said, watching her steadily.
"That's exactly what I'd like. I'd go up, and they'd judge me, and I'd burst out laughing in their faces. I'd dearly love to set fire to the house, Alyosha, our house — you still don't believe me?"
"Why not? There are children of twelve who feel a longing to set fire to something, and they do set things on fire. It's a kind of illness."
"That's not true, that's not true. There may be children like that, but that's not what I mean."
"You're mistaking evil for good — it's a passing crisis, maybe the result of your illness."
"You do despise me, though! It's simply that I don't want to do good, I want to do evil, and it has nothing to do with any illness."
"Why do evil?"

"So everything would be destroyed. Ah, how nice it would be if everything were destroyed! You know, Alyosha, sometimes I think about doing all sorts of terrible things, all sorts of evil, and I'd do it secretly for a long time, and then suddenly everyone would find out. Everyone would stand around and point their fingers at me, and I'd look right back at them all. That would be wonderful. Why would it be so wonderful, Alyosha?"
"I don't know. It's a craving to destroy something good, or, as you say, to set fire to something. It happens sometimes."
"I don't just say it — I'll actually do it."
"I believe you."
"Ah, how I love you for saying you believe me. And you're not lying, not one bit. But maybe you think I'm saying all this on purpose to annoy you?"
"No, I don't think that ... though maybe there's a little of that in it too."
"There's a little. I can never lie to you," she declared, a strange fire in her eyes.

What struck Alyosha most was her earnestness. There wasn't a trace of humor or teasing in her face now, though in the old days fun and high spirits never deserted her even in her most "earnest" moments.
"There are moments when people love crime," Alyosha said thoughtfully.

"Yes, yes! You've put my own thought into words — they love crime, everyone loves crime, they love it always, not just in 'moments.' You know, it's as if people agreed to lie about it and have been lying about it ever since. They all claim they hate evil, but secretly, every one of them loves it."
"And are you still reading those nasty books?"
"Yes, I am. Mamma reads them and hides them under her pillow, and I steal them."
"Aren't you ashamed of destroying yourself like this?"

"I want to destroy myself. There's a boy here who lay down between the railroad tracks while a train went past. Lucky fellow! Listen, your brother's on trial right now for murdering his father, and everyone loves that he killed his father."
"Loves that he killed his father?"
"Yes, loves it — everyone loves it! Everyone says how awful it is, but secretly they simply love it. I do, for one."
"There's some truth in what you say about everyone," Alyosha said softly.

"Oh, what ideas you have!" Lise shrieked with delight. "And you a monk, too! You wouldn't believe how much I respect you, Alyosha, for never lying. Oh, I have to tell you a funny dream of mine. I sometimes dream about devils. It's night, I'm in my room with a candle, and suddenly there are devils everywhere, in every corner, under the table, and they throw open the doors — there's a crowd of them behind the doors, and they want to come in and seize me. And they're just about to, just about to grab me. But I suddenly cross myself, and they all pull back, though they don't go away entirely — they stand at the doors and in the corners, waiting. And then suddenly I get a terrible urge to curse God out loud, and so I start, and then they come crowding back toward me, delighted, and seize me again, and I cross myself again, and they all pull back again. It's tremendous fun. It takes your breath away."
"I've had that exact same dream," Alyosha said suddenly.
"Really?" Lise cried, astonished. "I say, Alyosha, don't laugh — that's terribly important. Could two different people have the same dream?"
"It seems they can."

"Alyosha, I'm telling you, this is terribly important," Lise went on, in genuine amazement. "It's not the dream itself that matters, it's that you had the same dream as me. You never lie to me — don't lie now — is it true? You're not laughing?"
"It's true."
Lise seemed extraordinarily struck by this, and for half a minute she was silent.
"Alyosha, come see me — come see me more often," she said suddenly, in a pleading voice.
"I'll always come see you, all my life," Alyosha answered firmly.

"You're the only person I can talk to, you know," Lise began again. "I talk to no one but myself, and you. Only you in the whole world. And more easily to you than to myself. And I'm not the least bit ashamed with you, not the least bit. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed with you, not even a little? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?"
"I don't know."

"There's a book here where I read about a Jew put on trial — he took a child of four and cut the fingers off both its hands, then crucified it on the wall, hammered in nails and crucified it, and afterward, at his trial, he said the child died quickly, within four hours. That was 'quickly'! He said the child moaned, kept moaning, and he stood there admiring it. Isn't that nice?"
"Nice?"
"Nice. Sometimes I imagine it was me who crucified him. He'd hang there moaning and I'd sit across from him eating pineapple _compote_. I love pineapple _compote_ terribly. Do you like it?"
Alyosha looked at her without speaking. Her pale, sallow face suddenly twisted, her eyes burned.

"You know, when I read about that Jew, I shook with sobs all night. I kept imagining how the little thing cried and moaned — a child of four understands, you know — and the whole time the thought of pineapple _compote_ kept haunting me. In the morning I wrote a letter to a certain person, begging him particularly to come see me. He came, and I suddenly told him all about the child and the pineapple _compote_. All of it, all, and said it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice. Then he got up and left. He was here only five minutes. Did he despise me? Did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?" She sat up on the couch, eyes flashing.
"Tell me," Alyosha asked, anxious, "did you send for that person?"
"Yes, I did."
"Did you send him a letter?"
"Yes."
"Just to ask him about that, about the child?"
"No, not about that at all. But when he came, I asked him about it right away. He answered, laughed, got up, and left."
"That person behaved honorably," Alyosha murmured.
"And did he despise me? Did he laugh at me?"
"No — because he probably believes in the pineapple _compote_ himself. He's very ill right now too, Lise."
"Yes, he does believe in it," Lise said, her eyes flashing.
"He doesn't despise anyone," Alyosha went on. "He just doesn't believe anyone. And if he doesn't believe in people, of course he does despise them."
"So he despises me too, me?"
"You too."

"Good," Lise said, seeming almost to grind her teeth. "When he walked out laughing, I felt it was wonderful to be despised. The child with its fingers cut off is nice, and being despised is nice too...."
And she laughed in Alyosha's face, a feverish, malicious laugh.

"Do you know, Alyosha, do you know, I'd like — Alyosha, save me!" She suddenly sprang up from the couch, rushed to him, and grabbed him with both hands. "Save me!" she almost groaned. "Is there anyone else in the world I could tell what I've told you? I've told you the truth, the truth. I'll kill myself, because I loathe everything! I don't want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything. Alyosha, why don't you love me at all?" she finished, in a frenzy.
"But I do love you!" Alyosha answered warmly.
"And will you weep over me? Will you?"
"Yes."
"Not because I won't be your wife, but just weep for me?"
"Yes."

"Thank you! It's only your tears I want. Let everyone else punish me and trample me underfoot, everyone, everyone, not excepting a single one. Because I don't love anyone. Do you hear — not anyone! On the contrary, I hate him! Go, Alyosha, it's time you went to your brother"; she suddenly tore herself away from him.
"How can I leave you like this?" Alyosha said, almost alarmed.
"Go to your brother, the prison will be closing — go, here's your hat. Give my love to Mitya, go, go!"

And she practically shoved Alyosha out the door by force. He looked at her with pained surprise when he suddenly became aware of a letter in his right hand — a tiny letter, folded tight and sealed. He glanced at it and instantly read the address: "To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov." He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had turned almost threatening.
"Give it to him, you have to give it to him!" she ordered him, trembling and beside herself. "Today, at once, or I'll poison myself! That's why I sent for you."

And she slammed the door shut in an instant. The bolt clicked. Alyosha put the note in his pocket and went straight downstairs, without going back to Madame Hohlakov — he'd forgotten about her entirely, in fact. As soon as Alyosha was gone, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a crack, put her finger in the gap, and slammed the door with all her strength, pinching her finger. Ten seconds later, releasing her finger, she walked slowly, quietly to her chair, sat up straight in it, and stared intently at her blackened finger and the blood oozing out from under the nail. Her lips trembled, and she kept whispering rapidly to herself:
"I am a wretch, wretch, wretch, wretch!"
